notes.text: For 7 or 8, the skillet is very full. Toss slowly, and use the tongs to lift the pasta from the bottom.

move.title: Cheese, pepper, and pasta water
move.body: An emulsion is two things that don't normally mix, like fat and water, held together in one smooth, creamy sauce. Today you'll make cacio e pepe, a Roman pasta whose name means "cheese and pepper." The sauce is just cheese, black pepper, butter, and the starchy water the pasta cooked in.

why.title: Starchy water holds it together
why.body: Pasta lets starch out into its cooking water. That starch coats the tiny drops of melted cheese fat and keeps them from finding each other. Instead of separating into grease and lumps, they stay spread through the water as a creamy sauce. Less water in the pot means more starch in each cup.

why.title: Too hot makes clumps
why.body: Cheese melts smoothly when it's warm, but in a very hot pan its proteins squeeze together into rubbery strings and clumps. That's why the cheese goes in with the heat off, and why it's mixed into a paste with a little pasta water first.

why.title: Fine cheese melts fast
why.body: Cheese grated as fine as sand melts the moment it touches warm pasta. Thick shreds melt slowly, and while they wait, the outside gets too hot and clumps.

why.title: Toasting the pepper
why.body: Ground pepper warmed in butter for a minute smells stronger and tastes rounder. Its flavor dissolves in the fat, and the fat carries it all through the sauce.

wrong.fix: The pan was too hot. Add a splash of warm pasta water and toss hard off the heat. Small clumps often smooth out.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thick and pasty
wrong.fix: Toss in more pasta water, a splash at a time, until it's creamy and loose.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and watery
wrong.fix: Keep tossing for a minute. The starch thickens it as it cools a little. Add a little more cheese if it needs it.
Add a splash of pasta water and toss fast. The starch pulls the fat back into the sauce.

quiz.q: Why does the cheese go in with the heat off?
choices: Too much heat makes the cheese clump
quiz.explain: Very hot cheese turns rubbery and stringy. Warm pasta and water melt it smoothly.

quiz.q: What keeps the cheese fat and the water mixed together?
quiz.explain: The starch coats the little drops of fat so they stay spread through the sauce.

substitutions.note: Parmesan is a little milder and less salty. Taste at the end and add a pinch of salt if it needs it.
Gluten-free pasta water has less starch. Save extra water, and toss a little longer.

steps.text: Fill the large pot with the water, add the salt, cover it, and set it over high heat to come to a boil.
steps.tip: Fill the pot at the sink, then carry it to the stove before it's hot. Never carry a pot of boiling water.

steps.text: Put the grated cheese in the medium bowl. Fluff it with the fork to break up any clumps.
steps.tip: The cheese should look fine and powdery, like sand. If it's in thick shreds, chop it smaller.

steps.text: When the water is boiling hard, add the spaghetti and stir it with the tongs for the first two minutes so it doesn't stick. Cook it 2 minutes less than the box says.
steps.tip: It finishes cooking in the sauce, so it should still be a little firm now.

steps.text: While the pasta cooks, melt the butter in the skillet over medium-low heat. Add the pepper and stir until it smells toasty.
Put on an oven mitt. Dip the liquid measuring cup into the pasta pot and scoop out 2 cups of the cloudy water. Set it on the counter.
steps.tip: Hold the cup with the mitt. The water and the cup are very hot.

steps.text: Pour a few spoonfuls of the pasta water into the cheese and mash with the fork into a thick, smooth paste.
steps.tip: Wait a minute first so the water isn't boiling hot. Warm, not scalding, makes the smoothest paste.

steps.text: Pour about half a cup of pasta water into the skillet with the pepper. Use the tongs to lift the spaghetti straight from the pot into the skillet. Toss it for a minute over medium-low heat.
steps.tip: Let each tongful drip over the pot for a second before you carry it over.

steps.text: Turn off the heat under the skillet, and turn off the pasta pot too. Wait 30 seconds, then add the cheese paste. Toss fast and keep tossing, adding splashes of pasta water, until the sauce is smooth, creamy, and coats every strand.
steps.look: Glossy and creamy, like thin cream, with no clumps and no puddles of grease.

steps.text: Serve right away, with an extra grind of pepper on top.
steps.tip: Cacio e pepe thickens as it sits, so eat it hot. A splash of warm water loosens leftovers.
